note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Adult patient with 1 week of sore throat progressing to a dry cough, now with mild exertional shortness of breath and subjective wheeze; clinical impression most consistent with viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis. Symptomatic management advised and safety-netting provided; sick note issued.

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - Sore throat began ~7 days ago (Thu/Fri last week), dry cough started 1–2 days later.
  - Exertional shortness of breath began ~3–4 days ago; variable symptoms, not limiting activity; no rest dyspnea. Cough not worse at night.
  - Initially feverish for ~3 days, now resolved. Intermittent headaches. Decreased appetite without reported weight loss.
  - Denies sputum production and hemoptysis. Denies nasal/sinus congestion.
  - Reports subjective wheeze and some chest discomfort.
- Pertinent negatives mentioned:
  - No history of asthma. No history of venous thromboembolism (patient/family) reported. No known asbestos exposure. No recent significant travel.
- Past medical history:
  - Denies chronic conditions.
- Allergies:
  - Peanut allergy. Denies medication allergies.
- Medications:
  - None reported regularly; not currently taking medications.
- Family history:
  - Mother had lung cancer.
- Social and preventive:
  - Non-smoker (very rare past experimentation). Lives in the UK, born in the US. Employed; requested sick note.

Examination:
- Teleconsultation; no vitals obtained.
- Patient reports no palpable neck lumps/bumps.
- No objective physical examination findings available.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression:
  - Acute viral upper respiratory infection with acute bronchitis (high likelihood).
    - Supported by sore throat → dry cough sequence, initial transient fever, dry nonproductive cough, variable but non-severe course, exertional (not rest) dyspnea, and intermittent headache; no red flags such as hemoptysis or sustained high fever.
- Additional considerations (from DDx, consistent with transcript):
  - Post-viral reactive airway disease/new-onset asthma (medium likelihood): exertional SOB and subjective wheeze following a viral illness; no prior asthma history.
  - Atypical/early community-acquired pneumonia (low–medium): initial fever and chest discomfort, but currently afebrile, no sputum, and not systemically unwell.
  - Pulmonary embolism (low): exertional dyspnea/chest discomfort present but no risk factors and temporal link to viral symptoms.
- TB and primary lung cancer considered unlikely given acute viral prodrome, non-smoker status, and lack of red flags; reassurance provided.

Plan:
- Symptomatic management:
  - Paracetamol as needed for fever/discomfort.
  - Adequate fluids and rest.
- Work/administrative:
  - Sick note provided for additional days off work as requested.
- Safety net and follow-up:
  - Seek in-person GP assessment if symptoms worsen, particularly increased or sudden-onset breathlessness.
  - Expect improvement over the next 4–5 days; if not improving, contact a medical professional for reassessment.
  - Reassured regarding low likelihood of tuberculosis or lung cancer in this context; advised to re-present if persistent symptoms or new red flags develop.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  - No vitals (temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation), no objective chest or throat exam, no COVID-19/influenza status, no full review of systems, limited social history (alcohol/occupational exposures), and no specific follow-up appointment date set.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx/transcript:
  - DOB recorded as 09-May-2016 (pediatric) vs adult social history (employment) — conflict noted.
  - Shortness of breath initially denied then affirmed — internal transcript inconsistency noted.
  - Chest pain: patient reported “a bit of both” (wheeze and chest pain), later clinician phrased as “you don’t have any chest pain” — conflict noted.
● Transcript quality:
  - Teleconsultation with time constraints; limited history detail and no physical exam; some ambiguity and interruptions; end-of-call rushed with minimal closure.
